1	# Task 10: Fireworks display over a night harbor
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. The scene is a fireworks display at night over a calm harbor. Show a dark star-dusted night sky, a water surface that faintly reflects the light of the bursts, and a low dark silhouette of a shoreline or pier with a few small buildings or boats. Rockets launch from the shoreline one after another at irregular intervals, rise with a short glowing trail, and burst into spherical shells of many glowing sparks. Use at least three clearly different burst colors (for example gold, red, and blue or green), and make each burst fade and fall under gravity over a second or two before it disappears. Some bursts should leave trailing streaks. The sky and water should be lit subtly by the active bursts. The scene must animate continuously without user input, with a slow gentle camera drift or a fixed camera framing the sky and harbor. Aim for a polished, cinematic look: strong glow on the sparks against a dark background, no flat or washed-out colors, no visible geometry artifacts. Keep it smooth at interactive frame rates. Also expose window.__TASK_STATE__ = { bursts: <total number of bursts that have exploded so far>, activeParticles: <current number of live spark particles> } and update it every frame.

I'm realizing I could drive the spark particles with a GPU shader that computes position analytically from per-vertex burst center, velocity, and birth time against a time uniform, letting the CPU just track which particles are alive by counting elapsed time. That raises the question of how to pre-allocate burst geometry for dynamically spawned bursts.

I'm sketching a pool of around 8 reusable burst nodes, each holding billboard quad geometry for roughly 250 sparks, with mutable uniforms (origin, start time, color) and per-vertex attributes for random spark directions and speeds, using the view matrix's columns to build camera-facing right/up vectors for billboarding. For trailing streak effects, I'm considering rendering each spark as several fading ghost copies offset slightly earlier in time, encoded as extra per-vertex attributes.

Now I'm working out spark motion physics -- drag-adjusted velocity, gravity pulling sparks downward, randomized lifespans around 1.6-2.4 seconds, and fading alpha with a flicker effect plus shrinking size over the spark's life, while also accounting for rockets that rise before bursting.

For the rocket itself, I'm considering whether to fold it into the burst node system or give it a separate pool with its own trailing ghost quads tracing the ascent path, reusing the same shader structure as the burst ghosts but driving the position with an eased interpolation from launch point to apex.

I'm figuring out the per-vertex attributes needed—direction vector, life/ghost/size/phase info, and reusing the uv coordinate as the corner offset for the particle quad so I can compute radial falloff in the fragment shader. I also need to make sure the geometry's bounding box covers the full burst area so it doesn't get frustum-culled incorrectly.

content.thinking:
I'm considering keying uniforms by each pool node's runtime id so every node gets its own material instance, though a simpler alternative would be writing all bursts into a single node to avoid per-node uniform complexity.

Working out the pool sizing: a burst pool of 10 nodes with sparks and ghost copies, keeping inactive nodes cheap by pushing their geometry outside clip space rather than toggling draw calls, plus a smaller rocket pool. For lighting, I'm planning to pass active burst positions and colors as uniforms into custom sky and water shaders so they can subtly reflect nearby explosions instead of relying on real scene lights.

I'm also sketching the sky dome itself — a large unlit sphere with a gradient-plus-stars material that brightens near burst positions, feeding it the same packed light uniforms as the water, and relying on bloom alone for glow since there's no tonemapping preset in play.

For the stars, I'm converting the view direction into spherical coordinates and hashing grid cells to scatter twinkling points, sizing the cells so each star reads as roughly a single pixel at the target resolution.

For the water, I'm starting a large plane (200×200 units) positioned relative to the camera with a custom fragment shader for the base surface color.

The specular highlight compares the reflected view vector against the direction to the mirrored light, raised to a high power for a tight sparkly streak, plus a softer falloff glow term for cohesion. I'm also considering just drawing a mirrored copy of the burst nodes flipped below the water line for a more literal reflection effect.

For occlusion, I realize an opaque depth-writing water plane would naturally hide the mirrored sparks beneath it, but transparent water complicates draw-order sorting. The simpler fix is rendering mirrored sparks with depth testing disabled and slightly dimmed/wobbled, letting the shoreline silhouette layer draw over them to sell the illusion.

If the sky dome sits far behind everything with depth write off, mirrored sparks should stay occluded correctly by nearer silhouettes like the shoreline and pier. This adds complexity since I'm combining light-based reflections with mirrored sparks, but the visual payoff seems worth it, so I'll implement the mirror pass by duplicating the spark particles below the waterline.

Each burst now needs paired real and mirror nodes sharing the same geometry spec, doubling the node pool from 8 to 16, and I'm weighing whether to update each node's time uniform per frame individually or rely on a shared engine clock to avoid that overhead, settling on only updating uNow for active nodes each frame.

Alive-sparks counts per burst can just be computed on the CPU from the lifetime array, which is cheap even across 220 sparks per burst. For the mirror effect, I'll give it its own fixed uMirror uniform at material creation, and add a subtle sine-based horizontal ripple to the mirror sparks' world position to mimic water shimmer.

For the rocket, I'm using the same particle shader but modeling position as an exponential drag curve rather than constant velocity plus gravity -- solving for the launch velocity so the rocket decelerates naturally and reaches a target apex height within a chosen fuse time, with a slight horizontal lean added to the launch direction.

Now I'm defining the ghost-trail behavior (sampling earlier ages for shrinking, fading echoes) and the shared particle attributes/uniforms -- direction vector, life/ghost index/size variation packed into a vec4, and uniforms for age, origin, color, drag, gravity, and ghost spacing.

Writing the vertex shader logic to compute each particle's age offset by ghost index, decide aliveness based on life and trail spacing, then integrate position under drag and gravity falloff for the sparks.

I'm handling mirroring by flipping y across the waterline, hiding sparks once they sink below the surface, and fading intensity over the particle's lifetime with ghost trails dimming progressively further back.
